headline: High-risk write-capable OpenHands can conflict with a read-only knowledge list, but prompt-injection and leakage are limited by the pair’s lack of shared channels.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: awesome-selfhosted is non-runnable and exposes no I/O surfaces, so it cannot ingest OpenHands output by default. OpenHands can use files, browser, and MCP, but there is no shared channel or documented bridge between the pair. The pathway is therefore blocked absent external copy/paste or orchestration not shown in either profile.
conditions: IF an operator manually copies OpenHands output into awesome-selfhosted content workflows, prompt injection becomes possible.
IF a shared MCP server or clipboard bridge is added, attacker-controlled text can cross the boundary.
mitigations: Keep the agents disconnected; do not copy outputs between them.
Disable any shared clipboard or shared MCP server.
Review OpenHands outputs before manual reuse.
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging if a bridge is later introduced.

B_data_leakage.rationale: awesome-selfhosted touches no data classes and has no runtime I/O, while OpenHands reads and writes only files mounted into its runtime sandbox. With no shared workspace or authenticated principal shown, leakage is not a default pathway. The main risk is manual transfer of mounted-file contents into the knowledge-management side.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same mounted volume, OpenHands can expose file contents to the other workflow.
IF sensitive files are mounted into OpenHands and then copied into awesome-selfhosted artifacts, leakage occurs.
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent.
Do not mount sensitive files into OpenHands unless needed.
Restrict manual export from OpenHands to reviewed snippets only.
Rotate any secrets placed in the runtime after use.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: OpenHands has broad write and git-modifying capabilities inside its runtime, while awesome-selfhosted is read-only but can still be affected if both are pointed at the same mounted volume or repo. The pair does not document locking or coordination, so concurrent edits could clobber shared state if an operator configures overlap.
conditions: IF both agents are given write access to the same repository or mounted directory, concurrent modification conflicts can occur.
IF OpenHands is used to edit files that awesome-selfhosted also consumes as source data, state divergence can occur.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate directory.
Avoid concurrent edits to the same git branch.
Use a human merge step after OpenHands changes.
requires-engineering: add file-locking or branch isolation in orchestration.

D_cascading_error.rationale: OpenHands can generate code, browser-derived content, and file edits that a downstream workflow may treat as authoritative, while awesome-selfhosted can surface or curate that output without verification. Because no verification step is documented between them, the pair can propagate mistakes if OpenHands output is reused as trusted input.
conditions: IF OpenHands output is copied into awesome-selfhosted curation without review, incorrect facts can cascade.
IF OpenHands is used to draft content that another workflow publishes, downstream errors can persist.
mitigations: Require human review before reuse of OpenHands output.
Cross-check factual claims against primary sources.
Keep generated text separate from curated source lists.
requires-engineering: add automated verification gates before publication.

E_compliance.rationale: No specific residency or regulated data class is identified for awesome-selfhosted, while OpenHands explicitly handles files mounted into its runtime and model-provider API keys. The profiles do not show a direct compliance mismatch, but OpenHands’ secret handling means operators should avoid placing regulated data in mounted files without policy review.
conditions: IF regulated data is mounted into OpenHands and then exported into a separate workflow with different retention rules, compliance issues can arise.
IF a deployment policy forbids model-provider key handling in the same runtime as regulated files, the current setup violates that policy.
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of OpenHands mounts.
Store API keys separately from project files.
Confirm retention rules before copying outputs between agents.
requires-engineering: document a data-handling policy for the pair.
